segments.text: About once a minute during a recovery, a 20-ton jet comes down on a steel deck at around 240
kilometers an hour, and the moment its wheels touch, the pilot shoves the throttle to full power,
not to break, to fly away again. A hook under the tail is meant to snag a cable and stop the
aircraft in about two seconds, but if the hook misses, the pilot has to already be fast enough
to take off before the deck runs out. Every landing on a carrier begins with the pilot
planning to take off. So here is the question. A normal runway is two or three common dollars of
concrete that does not move. A carrier gives you about 300 meters of deck that pitches, rolls,
and runs away from you at 30 knots in an ocean where the nearest airfield may be a thousand common
dollars off. How does that become an airfield that launches and recovers dozens of aircraft a day?
The answer comes as a chain. Each part of a carrier exists because the part before it solved one
problem and handed over another. Start with the obvious one, which is that the deck is too short.
A fighter needs far more room than that to reach flying speed under its own power, so the carrier
does not let it try. A catapult tows the aircraft instead. On most large carriers, a piston driven
by steam runs along a slot under the deck, and a jet that weighs as much as 30 tons goes from standing
still to roughly 250 commilators an hour in about two seconds and around 100 meters. The newest
American carrier replaces steam with electromagnets, and the idea is the same. The ship does the work
so the aircraft does not have to. That solves taking off and creates the opposite problem,
which is stopping. Landing needs a stopping distance the deck does not have, so four steel
cables are stretched across it, and the pilot aims to catch the third. The cable pulls out against
hydraulic dampers below deck and takes the energy of a landing jet in about 100 meters. Everything in the
approach is built around that cable. The pilot flies at a fixed, slightly nose-high attitude,
watches a lit lens beside the deck for the right glide path, and a landing signal officer on the
deck calls corrections by radio. The lens is stabilized against the ship's own motion because the deck is
rising and falling by several meters under the approaching jet. At night, with no horizon, and a
deck the size of a car park, pilots describe the landing as one of the hardest things in military
flying. There is one more detail that changed the whole ship. In the early jet age, carriers had
straight decks, with aircraft parked at the front and the landing area at the back. A jet that missed
the wires flew straight into the parked aircraft. The fix, invented by the British in the early 1950s,
was to angle the landing area a few degrees off the ship's centerline. Now a missed landing,
called a bolter, simply keeps rolling off the end and goes around for another try, and the front of the
deck can be launching aircraft at the same moment other jets are landing. The angled deck is why the
full throttle trick works. Now the ship itself has a job in this, because an aircraft is easier to launch
into wind. A carrier turns into the wind and runs at full speed, so 30 knots of ship speed and a bit
of natural breeze put a steady stream of air over the deck before the jet has moved at all. That adds
free airspeed to every launch and takes away a lot of the speed the arresting gear has to absorb.
To keep that up through a day of flying, the ship needs engines that never get tired.
The largest carriers use nuclear reactors, which give them speed without a fuel tank to empty and
let the ship change course as often as flight operations need. There is a cost to that choice
that does not appear on the deck. A reactor frees the ship from its own fuel, but the aircraft still
need theirs. A carrier carries a floating stockpile of aviation fuel and bombs in magazines deep inside
the hull and jets burn through it quickly. So the real limit on a nuclear carrier is no longer the
ship. It is what the air wing can eat and what the ship can lift to the deck. That is where the
lifts come in. The flight deck is too small to park everything, so most aircraft live in a hangar below
and huge elevators carry them up and down at the side of the ship. A carrier is really two floors of
work. Below, mechanics repair, rearm, and refuel. Above, the deck crew moves aircraft in a narrow space that is
also a runway and a parking lot and a launch site all at once. Crews wear jerseys in different colors
so that a person glancing across a noisy deck can tell, from a hundred meters, whether someone
handles fuel, weapons, the catapult, or the wires. The sea adds attacks to all of this. Salt spray gets
into every joint and every connector, so aircraft that live on a carrier are washed, inspected, and
repaired far more than the same type kept on land. A deck that never stops being used also never stops
wearing, and the crew treats the steel the way a runway crew treats concrete. Weather decides what
is possible, too. If the deck pitches too far, the landing is simply canceled, and the aircraft head
for a divert field or a tanker. What the ship carries onto that deck is the point of the whole machine.
The air wing is a mix, and each type exists to cover a gap in another. Fighters and strike aircraft do the
shooting and bombing. A small radar aircraft with a rotating dish on top flies high and extends the
ship's view hundreds of kimeliers past the horizon. Helicopters hunt submarines and rescue pilots who
went into the sea. Electronic warfare aircraft blind enemy radar. Some of the strike aircraft carry fuel
tanks and hoses instead of weapons, because a jet that has just launched can be topped up in the air by
another jet from the same deck, and that is cheaper than building a longer ship. Taken together, the
wing is a way to see far, hit far and survive a bad day. Not every navy can afford a nuclear catapult
carrier, so there are cheaper answers, and each shows what it gave up. Some ships have no catapult and
use a curved ski jump on the bow, which flings a jet upward at flying speed. That works, but the aircraft
has to leave with less fuel and fewer weapons, so it flies a shorter mission. Others carry aircraft that can
take off almost vertically, which works without a long deck, but their range and load are smaller again.
The size of a carrier is a direct account of what it can launch. A carrier is also the most valuable
single target a navy owns, and the people who built it know that. The ship does not sail alone, it travels
inside a group of cruisers, destroyers and submarines, and the group's job is to put layers between an
attacker and the deck. Missiles and aircraft are tracked hundreds of kimelaters out, intercepted by escort
ships with their own missiles, and any submarine that gets close is hunted by helicopters and escorts
long before it can fire. The carrier itself carries some of its own defenses, but they are the last line,
not the first. There is a funny thing about the size of this machine. The largest carriers carry around 5,000
people, and the ship has its own bakery, its own hospital, its own post office, and its own news
channel. Aircraft are expensive, but a good share of that crew exists only so that the aircraft can be
fixed, fueled, and pointed at the sky. Even the settings are personal. Before each launch and each landing,
the crew sets the catapult and the arresting gear for the exact weight of that one aircraft, because a cable set
too soft lets a jet roll into the sea, and one set too hard can damage the aircraft or the cable. The whole system
is a chain of small, careful numbers. The whole ship is a very expensive way to deliver a very small number of
aircraft, to exactly the right place. Which brings us to what people often miss. We usually judge a
carrier by the aircraft count, but the number that matters is how many sorties it can generate each day,
and that depends on the deck cycle, how quickly it can launch, recover, refuel, rearm, and launch again.
That is my own reading, but it suggests that the real weapon is not the jet at all. It is the rhythm of
the deck, and the hundreds of people who keep it from missing a beat. So return to the pilot, coming in at
240 km an hour with the throttle already up. Every part of the ship, the catapult, the wires, the angled
deck, the reactor, and the hangar below, is there to make that one moment survivable and to make it
happen again a minute later. A carrier is not really a ship that carries aircraft. It is a machine for
taking off and landing, with a hull built around it.
